Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
 Mandatory 13
File
oracle-init/create-user.sh

Explanation

The product constructs all or part of an SQL command using externally-influenced input from an upstream component, but it does not neutralize or incorrectly neutralizes special elements that could modify the intended SQL command when it is sent to a downstream component. Without sufficient removal or quoting of SQL syntax in user-controllable inputs, the generated SQL query can cause those inputs to be interpreted as SQL instead of ordinary user data.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module, server-rendered Spring Boot application for uploading, browsing, viewing, and deleting photos. This assessment describes checked-in code and container configuration, not a verified running deployment; citations use repository-relative paths and line numbers. Credential values are omitted.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Browser - Bootstrap and upload JavaScript"] end subgraph App["Application Layer - Spring Boot 2.7.18 on Java 8"] Security["Spring Security - HTTP Basic"] Web["Spring MVC - HTML and JSON endpoints"] Views["Thymeleaf templates"] Services["Transactional photo business logic"] Images["ImageIO - image header inspection"] end subgraph Data["Data Access and Storage"] JPA["Spring Data JPA - Hibernate and Oracle JDBC"] Oracle[("Oracle Database - PHOTOS metadata and BLOBs")] Volume[("Oracle data volume")] end subgraph External["External Services"] CDN["jsDelivr - Bootstrap assets"] end Browser -->|"HTTP on port 8080 - pages, photos, multipart uploads"| Security Security -->|"Public reads and authenticated upload or delete"| Web Web -->|"Page models"| Views Views -->|"Rendered HTML"| Browser Web -->|"Upload, lookup, navigation and deletion"| Services Services -->|"Validate image dimensions"| Images Services -->|"Read and write entities"| JPA JPA -->|"Oracle SQL over JDBC on port 1521"| Oracle Oracle -->|"Compose persistent storage"| Volume Web -->|"JSON upload results and binary image responses"| Browser Browser -->|"HTTPS CSS and JavaScript requests"| CDN

Technology Stack Summary

LayerTechnologyVersionPurpose
Runtime and packagingJava, Maven, executable Spring Boot JARJava 8; Boot 2.7.18; application 1.0.0One application process, bootstrapped by PhotoAlbumApplication (pom.xml:8-26,103-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14).
PresentationSpring MVC, ThymeleafBoot-managed; no independent versions declaredGallery/detail HTML, JSON upload response, binary photo delivery (pom.xml:30-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-57; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-83).
BrowserBootstrap and plain JavaScript Fetch APIBootstrap 5.3.0CDN-hosted styling/widgets; multipart uploads and dynamic gallery updates (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124-125; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:97-111,178-185).
SecuritySpring Security, BCrypt, in-memory user storeBoot-managed; no independent version declaredStateless HTTP Basic; authenticated POST upload/delete, public remaining requests, CSRF disabled (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61).
Business logicSpring services, transaction management, JDK ImageIOBoot-managed Spring; JDK 8 APIUpload validation, header-based dimension inspection, navigation, persistence orchestration (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-47,81-174,221-237).

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the application datastore: Photo maps to photos, combining UUID identifiers, file metadata, timestamps, dimensions, and a @Lob byte array (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-97). Uploads save image bytes through the repository; image responses read those bytes directly, rather than retrieving uploaded files from disk (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-174; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:57-83). The /uploads/ path is compatibility metadata, not the current image-serving path. Compose connects the application and Oracle over a bridge network, waits for database health, and mounts oracle_data; both application profiles configure Hibernate schema creation at startup, so a persistent volume alone does not ensure retention across application restarts (docker-compose.yml:12-22,30-51; src/main/resources/application.properties:17-20; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-16).

The browser fetches Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:7,147). No cache, message broker, object-storage service, or outbound business API integration was identified in the inspected application sources and configuration. Database and administrator credential values are not reproduced.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: all three controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its single implementation depends on PhotoRepository. Transaction boundaries live in the service, with read-only lookup/navigation operations (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-32; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-32; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-71,223-237).
  • Database-backed image storage with Oracle coupling: metadata and BLOB bytes share one entity, and native queries use Oracle constructs including ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:34-87).
  • Public gallery with protected mutations: Spring Security authenticates upload/delete POST routes using HTTP Basic and an injected administrator configuration; it uses an in-memory user store and stateless sessions, with CSRF explicitly disabled (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61).

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application exposes five explicit controller endpoints: two HTML reads, one binary photo read, one multipart JSON upload, and one form-based deletion. Browser requests and database operations are synchronous; no service-to-service HTTP API or asynchronous messaging implementation was found.

Evidence references below use repository-relative paths and line numbers. Credential values are intentionally omitted.

Contract details

  • Upload processing is sequential and returns HTTP 200 even when every processed file fails; clients must inspect success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads. A successful service result is re-read by ID before being included in the response (HomeController.java:68-97). Service-level rejections are represented as per-file errors, not automatically HTTP 400 (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:82-109,138-154,172-192).
  • Upload transport limits are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request; oversized multipart requests can be rejected before the controller. No custom exception-to-status mapping for that case was found, so no exact status is promised here (src/main/resources/application.properties:23-25). Detailed validation rules belong in business-workflows.md.
  • The binary response adds Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size headers (PhotoFileController.java:74-83).
  • No URL/header/query API versioning is implemented in the controller mappings. The browser's _t query argument is cache busting, not versioning, and is not bound by the photo controller (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179; PhotoFileController.java:37-38).
  • Static CSS, JavaScript, and a bundled upload image also exist under src/main/resources/static; these are framework-served assets rather than additional declared business controller endpoints. No JSON resource-list/read/delete REST endpoints are declared.

There are no gateway-level DTOs, Java records, protobuf schemas, GraphQL schemas, or checked-in OpenAPI specifications in the inspected application sources. JSON serialization relies on Spring MVC/Jackson defaults through the web/JSON starters; no custom mapper, serializer, or explicit date format was found (pom.xml:31-35,75-79; HomeController.java:56-58,79). HTML rendering uses Thymeleaf rather than serializing the entire Photo model (pom.xml:37-41; DetailController.java:44-54). Entity fields and persistence details belong in data-architecture.md, not this inventory.

The upload response's compatibility filePath is not the implemented binary endpoint: the service constructs a legacy /uploads/ path, while the browser builds /photo/{id} from the returned ID (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-167; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179).

Communication Patterns

  • Browser-to-application: Same-origin HTTP requests; upload uses fetch('/upload') with FormData, parses JSON, and updates the gallery. Delete uses an HTML POST form; images use /photo/{id} (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:97-126,176-185; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50,67).
  • Within the application: Controllers invoke injected PhotoService; PhotoServiceImpl invokes PhotoRepository synchronously under transactions. Upload saves a photo, then the controller performs another lookup for the response projection. These are in-process layers, not independently deployed microservices (HomeController.java:28-31,68-83; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-47,69-75,172-184; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-16).
  • External data communication: JDBC to Oracle using the Compose DNS hostname oracle-db and port 1521; this is database protocol traffic, not REST (docker-compose.yml:30-34; src/main/resources/application.properties:9-15).
  • External browser dependencies: Templates load Bootstrap CSS/JavaScript from jsDelivr over HTTPS. This is browser asset retrieval, not a server-side business service API (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7,124).
  • Async: No message broker, event bus, queue producer/consumer, or application background messaging implementation found. JavaScript async/await is client request handling, not an asynchronous service communication contract (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90-132; pom.xml:30-101).
  • Resilience and timeouts: No explicit HTTP-client/JDBC request timeout, retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, or downstream fallback library/configuration was found in the application. Browser upload has one fetch attempt and no explicit timeout or abort handling; failures show feedback without retry (upload.js:102-132). Gallery reads fall back to an empty list; detail failures redirect; photo-serving failures return 500; upload failures become per-file results (HomeController.java:38-49,85-97; DetailController.java:38-58; PhotoFileController.java:84-86). A transaction completion failure can still escape the upload method/controller; the per-file envelope is not a universal error handler (PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-29,81-82,172-192).
  • Discovery, gateway, balancing: No Eureka/Consul registration, API gateway, response composition across backend services, or client-side load balancing found. Compose supplies ordinary container-name DNS; there is one application service (docker-compose.yml:1-44; pom.xml:30-101).
  • Availability: Compose starts the application after the database is healthy and restarts the application on failure; this is process orchestration, not per-request retry. See configuration-inventory.md for startup configuration (docker-compose.yml:39-44).
  • Security posture: Public reads; POST /upload and /detail/*/delete require HTTP Basic authentication. A single in-memory administrative user is created with BCrypt password encoding and an ADMIN role, but endpoint rules check only authentication, not that role. Authentication is stateless and CSRF is explicitly disabled. No JWT/OAuth2 or method-level role checks were found (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61). The application publishes HTTP 8080, with no checked-in HTTPS listener or TLS enforcement; external ingress TLS cannot be inferred. No JDBC TLS requirement is expressed by the configured connection URL (docker-compose.yml:32,37-38; src/main/resources/application.properties:1-15). Credential values are not reproduced here.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose interpolation → Oracle/application configuration: resolve required ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD before starting services. Missing/empty required inputs fail Compose interpolation (docker-compose.yml:7-9,34-36).
  2. Oracle container → database initialization: mount oracle-init into /container-entrypoint-initdb.d and persist data in oracle_data. User creation/grant scripts consume credentials or expect the configured schema user; SQL grant/verification files retain a fixed user identifier and must stay aligned with APP_USER (docker-compose.yml:12-14; oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:3-30; oracle-init/02-verify-user.sql:4-12; oracle-init/create-user.sh:11-44).
  3. Application → waits for → healthy Oracle: Compose uses depends_on.oracle-db.condition=service_healthy. Oracle runs the image-provided healthcheck.sh every 30s, timeout 10s, 15 retries, start period 180s. The separate oracle-init/healthcheck.sql is not the Compose health-check command (docker-compose.yml:17-22,39-41; oracle-init/healthcheck.sql:1-3).
  4. Application context → datasource and required admin/upload settings: Boot starts the application and initializes configured beans; datasource/admin password inputs are required outside the test profile. The application container restarts on failure; no application-level readiness probe, custom datasource retry/backoff, or startup timeout is declared (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:41-47; docker-compose.yml:44).
  5. Azure script sequencing, separate from Compose: existing Azure CLI authentication → resource group → registry → AKS → registry attachment → PostgreSQL → database/firewall → 30-second delay → user/grants → .env. This is infrastructure provisioning, not a checked-in application deployment/readiness chain (azure-setup.ps1:45-58,69-105,117-197,207-299).

The Oracle shell helper uses a fixed 30-second sleep rather than a readiness polling loop (oracle-init/create-user.sh:15-17). No config-server/discovery-server dependency exists in the inspected configuration.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local/Compose: operator copies .env.example to ignored .env and supplies credentials → Compose interpolation validates required password variables → Oracle receives its administrative/application credentials → the Java container receives datasource and administrator variables. Spring resolves datasource placeholders and relaxed environment binding for app.admin.* (.env.example:1-17; .gitignore:201-204; docker-compose.yml:7-9,31-36; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-42).
  • Oracle access: the image creates the configured application user; checked-in SQL grants schema privileges and the shell helper can create the user through an administrative session. Fixed user identifiers in SQL are not dynamically driven by APP_USER; changing that environment variable alone does not update those scripts (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:3-30; oracle-init/create-user.sh:21-35).
  • Application access: administrator credentials create an in-memory user; BCrypt encoding is applied. This is application password hashing, not encryption of environment variables or .env (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-42).
  • Azure provisioning: uses an already authenticated Azure CLI context; accepts environment-provided passwords or generates them with a cryptographic random-number generator. PostgreSQL administration creates/grants application access; the application password is exported and persisted in plaintext .env. The script's completion output also includes a password-bearing output location; no value is reproduced here (azure-setup.ps1:15-22,38-45,207-257,274-299,319).
  • Registry access: provisioning enables the registry administrator and attaches ACR to AKS. No application Key Vault binding, explicit secret-specific managed-identity/RBAC role assignment, Jasypt encryption, sealed secret, or secret rotation procedure is declared (azure-setup.ps1:69-74,102-105; pom.xml:30-100).
  • Automation/developer tooling: workflow tokens are obtained from GitHub secret references; example MCP credentials are process environment settings. Neither is evidence of a cloud application secret provisioning pipeline.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse uploaded photos, inspect individual images, and move through the collection chronologically. Authenticated operators can add multiple photos and permanently remove photos from the shared gallery.

Evidence references below use repository-relative paths and source line numbers. No credential values are reproduced.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto managementAn uploaded image together with information needed to display, identify, and navigate it. This is the only persisted business entity identified; there are no separate album, owner, or tag entities.Image content and descriptive information belong to the same photo. Older/newer neighbors are calculated from upload time, not stored relationships.
UploadResultPhoto intakeA transient operation outcome, not a persisted entity: communicates whether an individual photo was accepted and associates success with the resulting photo or failure with an explanation.Links a submitted filename to a saved Photo identifier or an error.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:12-19,28-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:220-238.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with internal components, not separately deployed domain services. The bounded contexts below are descriptive responsibility groupings, not explicit DDD modules.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
HomeControllerGallery presentation and batch intakeNo independent ownership; composes Photo information and per-file outcomesInternal PhotoService
DetailControllerIndividual viewing and removalNo independent ownership; reads/deletes Photo through the serviceInternal PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerImage deliveryNo independent ownership; serves Photo contentInternal PhotoService
PhotoServiceImplPhoto lifecycle and admission policyPhoto lifecycle; transient UploadResultPhotoRepository and image-header readers
PhotoRepositoryPhoto persistenceAuthoritative persisted Photo collection, including image contentDatabase; queries use Oracle-specific SQL

All controllers share the same service and repository; no inter-domain identifier exchange, independent service-owned databases, gateway, or event bus appears in the traced workflows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-32,68-83; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27,38-52,64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-32,44-83; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-48,160-174; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-27,34-56.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Add multiple photos with independent outcomes

  1. An operator selects or drops files into the gallery. The browser applies Client upload screening, then submits the remaining files together through POST /upload and displays progress. Authentication is required by Mutation authorization.
  2. HomeController applies Nonempty batch and processes each file sequentially through PhotoService rather than opening one batch-wide transaction.
  3. PhotoService applies Server upload admission and Image-header inspection. A rejected file normally produces an UploadResult failure and does not prevent later files from being considered.
  4. For an accepted file, the service generates a compatibility filename/path, reads content, captures available dimensions, constructs Photo, and saves it. The generated compatibility path is not a filesystem write.
  5. On service success, the controller re-fetches the photo by its returned identifier and adds presentation metadata to the successful-results list. Failures are collected separately. Batch outcome calculation determines the overall success flag.
  6. The browser prepends successful cards to the gallery and displays individual failure messages. It requests image bytes separately by photo identifier; it does not display images from the compatibility upload path.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-131,135-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-60; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-192.

Failure boundaries matter: upload failures caught inside the service become per-file results, but the controller does not catch exceptions from the successful-upload re-fetch or from a transactional proxy at commit. Those exceptions can terminate the request after earlier files have already been committed. A successful save whose re-fetch returns empty is included in neither result list. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,172-192.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate individual photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController loads the complete collection using Gallery ordering and renders photo cards.
  2. If collection retrieval fails, the controller renders an empty collection instead. The template's empty-gallery message therefore cannot distinguish a genuinely empty album from a loading failure.
  3. Selecting a card opens GET /detail/{id}. DetailController finds the requested photo, then asks the service for older and newer neighbors using Chronological navigation.
  4. The detail view shows metadata, conditionally available dimensions, and only the neighbor links that have a target. Blank identifiers, absent photos, or lookup/navigation exceptions redirect to the gallery.
  5. Gallery/detail image elements independently request GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController applies Image delivery availability, returning stored bytes and the recorded media type when present. Its no-cache response makes subsequent views request content again.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:18-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-108; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94,103-130.

Workflow 3: Permanently remove a photo

  1. The detail view offers a delete form with a browser confirmation prompt. This is a user-interface safeguard, not a server-side approval step.
  2. An authenticated operator submits POST /detail/{id}/delete; Mutation authorization applies.
  3. PhotoService looks up the photo and applies Delete existence. An existing photo is deleted from the repository, including its stored content; an absent photo returns a negative outcome.
  4. DetailController sets a success, not-found, or failure flash message and redirects to the gallery, which displays that message.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:54-60; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:195-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:37-46.

Other entry points

The application entry point only starts the application; no business-state seeding is present there. No scheduled tasks, business event listeners, or batch runners were identified in the inspected Java sources. Repository methods for monthly selection, pagination, and statistics exist, but the traced service/controllers do not expose business workflows using them; they are not documented as active user features. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:58-100; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:50-238.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend-to-backend service calls or gateway aggregation in the inspected application. Browser requests flow through local controllers and PhotoService to the shared PhotoRepository. The database is the source of truth for both photo descriptions and bytes; there is no separate object-storage lookup in the actual serving path. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:160-174; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-83.

Composition occurs locally in two places:

  • Upload response: HomeController joins each successful UploadResult to a newly fetched Photo by identifier and emits a metadata collection alongside a separate failures collection. The browser joins metadata to image content through identifier-based image requests, not through the returned compatibility path. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-95; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:113-120,176-185.
  • Detail page: DetailController combines the selected Photo with two optional neighbor identifiers from separate service reads. There is no common read transaction spanning all three calls, so navigation is not guaranteed to reflect a single snapshot during concurrent changes. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-52; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:67-76,223-238.

No circuit breaker, retry, event-driven reconciliation, or external-service fallback appears in these paths. Actual degradation is local: collection failure becomes an empty gallery; detail failure redirects home; missing bytes become not-found; other image-serving exceptions become a server error. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:39-48; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:48-86.

Business Workflow Sequence

Primary process: upload a collection of photos and make accepted images visible. Participants represent local components, not microservices. Rules and failure boundaries are supported by the Workflow 1 citations above.

sequenceDiagram actor Operator participant Browser as "Gallery browser" participant Access as "Access control" participant Home as "Upload controller" participant Service as "Photo service" participant Photo as "New Photo" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" Operator->>Browser: Select or drop photos Browser->>Browser: Screen selected files Browser->>Access: Submit acceptable files alt Caller is not authenticated Access-->>Browser: Authentication required Browser-->>Operator: Upload failed else Caller is authenticated Access->>Home: Pass upload batch Home->>Home: Require a nonempty batch loop Each submitted file Home->>Service: Request photo admission Service->>Service: Check upload and image-header rules alt File rejected or read fails Service-->>Home: File failure with explanation else File accepted Service->>Photo: Assign identity and upload time Service->>Store: Save photo content and description alt Save succeeds Store-->>Service: Saved Photo Service-->>Home: Success with photo identity Home->>Service: Retrieve saved photo Service->>Store: Find Photo by identity Store-->>Service: Photo Service-->>Home: Photo metadata Home->>Home: Add metadata to successful results else Save raises an error inside service Service-->>Home: File failure with explanation end end end Home-->>Browser: Successful photos and individual failures Browser-->>Operator: Show new cards and upload feedback Note over Browser,Store: Image bytes are fetched separately by photo identity end

The diagram shows handled per-file failures, not a guarantee of continued execution after a commit-time or re-fetch exception. Those unhandled request-level boundaries are described in Workflow 1.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Admission and validation

  • Nonempty batch: A null or empty bound list returns a bad-request response with overall failure. Multipart binding/transport rejection may occur before the controller executes. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-66.
  • Client upload screening: The browser allows JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP MIME types, rejecting files larger than 10 MiB. It does not reject zero-length files here. Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-88.
  • Server upload admission: Declared MIME type, lowercased, must be in the configured allowlist; size must be positive and no greater than the configured maximum. Current configuration specifies the same four MIME types and 10,485,760-byte limit; multipart transport limits are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request. A missing MIME type reaches the generic upload-error catch, rather than a dedicated validation result. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:41-47,86-110,186-190; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30.
  • Image-header inspection: When an ImageIO reader recognizes the content, width multiplied by height above 40,000,000 pixels rejects the upload. An I/O exception rejects the file; other inspection exceptions log a warning and permit continuation without dimensions. If no reader recognizes the content, acceptance can continue with absent dimensions, so MIME admission is not proof of valid image content. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:34-35,117-158.
  • Photo metadata constraints: Entity annotations require nonblank original/stored filenames of at most 255 characters, positive nonnull file size, nonblank MIME type of at most 50 characters, nonnull upload time, and a compatibility path of at most 500 characters. These are declared entity constraints, not explicit controller validation steps. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:28-79.
  • Configured versus enforced count: Configuration declares a maximum of ten files per upload, but the controller loops over the entire supplied list and PhotoService does not consult that property. Do not treat ten files as an enforced business constraint. Evidence: src/main/resources/application.properties:30; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:57-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:37-48.

Decisions, derived values, and lifecycle

  • Batch outcome calculation: Overall success means at least one photo appears in the successful-results list, not that every file succeeded. A nonempty processed batch normally returns HTTP success even when every individual file failed. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97.
  • Identity and lifecycle: New Photo instances receive a UUID and current local upload time. A separate UUID-based stored filename retains the submitted extension, and a compatibility path is derived from it. The observable lifecycle is submitted → rejected or persisted → deleted; no approval, soft deletion, recovery, deduplication, or ownership relationship is implemented in the traced model/service. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:93-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-185,195-217,243-248.
  • Gallery ordering / Chronological navigation: Gallery entries are newest first. Previous means the closest strictly older upload; next means the closest strictly newer upload, chosen as the first query result. Equal timestamps are excluded from both directions; no secondary ordering is specified. Missing neighbors suppress navigation links. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:18-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:220-238; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:74-94.
  • Image delivery availability: Blank/missing identifiers and absent or empty content produce not-found; serving exceptions produce a server error. The recorded MIME type controls the response content type. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86.
  • Delete existence: Only an existing photo can be removed; a nonexistent identifier yields false rather than a successful deletion. There is no downstream file-deletion or compensation step because content belongs to the persisted photo. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:199-217.
  • Presentation-derived values: Gallery/detail views format upload dates and file sizes and show dimensions only when available; these are display calculations, not additional persisted lifecycle states. Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:161-197; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:108-130.

Cross-cutting business behavior

  • Mutation authorization: Upload and delete require authentication; gallery, details, and content are public. The configured account is assigned an administrative role, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than that role. There are no resource-owner checks in the traced controllers. Authentication is stateless HTTP Basic; CSRF checking is disabled. Credential values are intentionally omitted. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-60.
  • Transactions and consistency: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transaction scope; retrieval and neighbor methods are read-only. Each controller-invoked upload is a separate service transaction, not an atomic batch. Local database exceptions are sometimes converted into failure results, but commit errors can arise after the service method returns; a result flag alone does not establish a successful commit. There is no saga or cross-service compensation in these flows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,53-75,172-192,198-217,223-238; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97.
  • Errors and observability: Read/delete service failures are wrapped as runtime exceptions; upload generally reports a per-file explanation. Upload and deletion successes and failures are logged, and file delivery logs include metadata and a prefix of image bytes. These operational logs are not an identified durable business audit trail; no dedicated audit entity or business exception hierarchy appears in the inspected workflows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-75,179-190,201-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:54-72.

Version-management evidence: The local POM declares org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-parent:2.7.18, with no local BOM import or version overrides for the starters, Oracle, or H2 (pom.xml:8–13, 23–101). Build boundary: Java 8 source/target and java.version=1.8 are explicitly configured (pom.xml:23–28). No Maven/Gradle multi-module declaration or recognized package lockfile was found. Analysis inspected build/package files only; no source inspection or build/test execution was performed.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is the final 2.x open-source maintenance release and represents a legacy baseline; commercial support terms must be checked separately. Moving to Boot 3 requires Java 17 or newer and migration from Java EE javax APIs to Jakarta APIs, while this build explicitly targets Java 8 (pom.xml:8–13, 23–28). The inherited BOM still manages older framework families (Spring Framework 5.3.31, Hibernate 5.6.15.Final, and Spring Security 5.7.11); these are managed versions, not separately declared or verified resolved dependencies. Review the pinned Commons IO 2.11.0 and Oracle JDBC 21.5.0.0 during modernization. This dependency inventory is not a vulnerability scan and does not establish current CVE status.

Notable Observations

  • The parent centralizes nearly all versions; Commons IO alone is explicitly pinned locally, so its upgrade must be considered separately from parent upgrades (pom.xml:8–13, 68–73).
  • spring-boot-starter-json is declared under an “Image processing” comment, but its artifact identifies JSON support, not an image-processing library. Web and JSON starters can overlap transitively; no resolved dependency tree was produced (pom.xml:31–35, 75–79).
  • Oracle is runtime-scoped while H2 is test-scoped, indicating different database dependencies between runtime and tests; SQL/dialect equivalence cannot be inferred from declarations (pom.xml:49–54, 88–93).
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope, not runtime scope. Its presence is development tooling, and it remains included in the non-test declaration count (pom.xml:95–100). No direct messaging, caching, logging, or observability dependency is declared; starter-provided transitives are deliberately not counted.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate to Oracle; H2 is configured for tests. Image bytes and metadata share the same database row rather than separate object storage (pom.xml:43-54,88-93; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91).

  • No explicit connection-pool sizing, timeout tuning, or alternative pool provider is present in those datasource files. The JPA starter normally supplies HikariCP through its dependency chain; no explicit Hikari configuration or resolved dependency report was found in the inspected source.
  • Oracle scripts grant schema-scoped creation privileges and tablespace quota, then verify the account; they do not create or seed photos (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:14-30; oracle-init/02-verify-user.sql:4-12). No schema/data/import SQL scripts were found under src, and no programmatic seeding was found in the inspected Java source.
  • Startup schema recreation is destructive rather than a versioned migration strategy. H2 context loading alone does not establish Oracle-query portability: repository SQL uses Oracle ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR, and the entity includes Oracle-specific column definitions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:34-87; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:61-79).

Entity Model

Photo maps to photos and defines a non-unique upload-timestamp index. All ten persistent fields appear above; Java types are String, byte[], Long, LocalDateTime, and nullable Integer dimensions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91). Nullability and lengths in the diagram describe database mappings, not the separate business validation rules.

The constructor generates the UUID and application timestamp; the timestamp column also declares an Oracle current-timestamp default. There is no generated sequence identifier, foreign key, association mapping, cascade, relationship fetch strategy, or optimistic-lock version field in this entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:24-97). photoData has @Lob but no explicit lazy-fetch annotation; native listing queries select the BLOB along with metadata (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:36-41; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:22-27). The diagram has no relationship edges because no second persisted entity exists; none are inferred from filenames.

UploadResult is an unannotated response object, not another database entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-10).

Transactions are declared at PhotoServiceImpl class scope, with read-only overrides for listing, ID lookup, and previous/next lookups. Upload and delete inherit the class transaction; upload catches persistence exceptions internally, so a returned result is not proof of successful transaction commit (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,53-75,172-193,198-217,223-237).

Data Ownership Boundaries

The inspected Maven project defines one application module, one entity and one repository, not multiple independently owned databases. Metadata and image contents are colocated in the same application schema and row; test execution substitutes an isolated ephemeral H2 database (pom.xml:15-18; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-91; src/test/resources/application-test.properties:1-9).

The service accesses its own database through PhotoRepository; there is no cross-service database access, remote data aggregation, or separate command/read-store implementation in the inspected persistence layer. Reads and writes share the same entity and repository. Image content is read into a byte array and saved as a BLOB; the stored path and generated filename are compatibility metadata, not evidence of an active filesystem-backed image store (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174,198-210). Serving reads the BLOB from the entity rather than reading that path (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-69).
